newsitem.title: LAOS: Laos hit with sharp rise in 1996 trade deficit.
newsitem.headline: Laos hit with sharp rise in 1996 trade deficit.

text.p: Newly released figures on Laos' economy show that 1996 brought a 50 percent increase in the small nation's trade deficit and a modest slowdown in economic growth, a U.N. economist said on Tuesday.

In real terms, the Laotian economy grew 6.8 percent in 1996 versus seven percent in 1995, and against a forecast of eight to 8.5 percent for 1997, U.N. Development Programme senior economist Romeo Reyes told Reuters.
The UNDP figures were based on raw government statistics.
Reyes said the slowdown was mainly caused by low growth in the agriculture sector and the worst flooding in years, which led to a 200,000-tonne rice deficit.
Agriculture accounts for 60 percent of Laos' annual Gross Domestic Product (GDP), Reyes said.
Reyes said other bad news in 1996 included the closure of 14 garment factories, which helped to spur the trade deficit increase from $243 million in 1995 to $365 million in 1996.
He said the manufacturers closed their doors when Laos lost trade preferences with the European Union last year.
Garment exports dropped from $77 million in 1995 to $65 million in 1996.
There were some positive signs. The leading export, wood, rose from $88 million in 1995 to $127 million in 1996, while hydroelectric electric exports rose $24 million to $31 million, Reyes said.
The government has said it expects continuing growth in hydropower to spur much of Laos' future growth.
Coffee, which rose from $3 million to $21.3 million from 1994-5 with a doubling of volume and trebling of price, continued its growth, though less spectacularly, to $22.5 million in 1996, Reyes said.
Imports increased 15 percent, from $589 million in 1995 to $678 million in 1996, while per capita GDP rose from $315 in 1995 to $385, Reyes said.

In December 1996, inflation had slowed to 7.2 percent after peaking at nearly 30 percent mid-year, but Reyes predicted more monetary turbulence in the future due to the lack of foreign exchange from the sizeable trade deficit.
As of February this year, inflation climbed back to 10 percent and the kip depreciated from 980 to the dollar in December 1996 to 1080 in May, Reyes said.
